why: Counting coin combinations teaches that loop order decides what is counted: with coins in the outer loop each multiset is built in one fixed coin order, so it counts combinations; with amounts in the outer loop every ordering is counted separately.
hints: Why does ways[a] = sum of ways[a - c] over all coins give the wrong answer here? Count [1,2] and [2,1] for amount 3.
Fix the coin order: first decide how many 1s, then how many 2s, and so on. Putting the coin loop outside does exactly that.
ways[0] = 1; for each coin c, for a from c up to amount: ways[a] += ways[a - c]. The upward sweep allows reuse. O(coins * amount).
pitfalls: Swapping the loops counts permutations (Combination Sum IV), not combinations.
Amount 0 has exactly one combination, even when no coin fits.
Looping a downward would allow each coin at most once.
